title: Teacher training; practice teaching
description: Edith 'Bobby' Cooney describes her two-year course at Lewiston State Normal School, where she studied rural education and nearly failed Palmer Method penmanship. She recalls practice teaching at a two-room country school outside Lewiston, living with five other student teachers and a supervisor, doing chores, and making a lifelong friend.

title: Married women barred from teaching; school board scrutiny
description: She explains that after the war, married women were seldom hired as teachers and tells of a neighbour who hid her marriage to keep her job. She also recounts a school board member who asked if she danced before grudgingly hiring her.

title: Biographical details; early cars
description: Jeanne Scott records Bobby's full name, birth in 1906 in Almira, Washington, and her family's move to Latah County as an infant. They discuss the family's early cars, a Baby Grand and a Gardner.

title: Parents; sister's death; siblings
description: Bobby identifies her mother as Wiley and her father as John Fletcher, born in Indiana. She recounts how her parents left Iowa after her little sister was killed in a farm accident, a loss her mother never discussed, and names her brothers and sisters.

title: Courtship and marriage
description: She and the interviewer discuss her husband Ernest, born in Anamoose, North Dakota in 1907, their wedding on his farm in 1934 with a chicken dinner, and their honeymoon at Lake Coeur d'Alene. They lived in Moscow eight years while he worked as a butter maker before returning to the farm.

title: Children; backtracking to school dates
description: Bobby names her two sons Gary and Don and their occupations, then she and Jeanne correct the dates and name of her normal school, Lewiston State Normal School, which she first attended in 1925-26.

title: Happy childhood; hand-me-downs; farm play
description: Bobby remembers a happy childhood as the middle child, playing outdoors with her younger brothers while her older sisters worked in the house. She recalls crying over an ugly hand-me-down coat and being delighted by a signet ring for her twelfth birthday.

title: High school in Palouse; mother's table
description: She describes riding the train to board in Palouse for high school at fourteen and coming home weekends for her mother's cooking. Her mother fed hired men and all comers, and the children giggled at the hired men's table habits until sent away.

title: Country school; becoming a teacher
description: She recalls walking to the country school she attended and later taught in, and boarding near the last school where she taught. After working in a Potlatch boarding house, she decided to become a teacher, overcoming homesickness once she chose the path herself.

title: Family life then and now
description: Comparing generations, Bobby feels her sons' families keep the same closeness, shared meals and good manners she grew up with. She recalls her family's self-sufficient farm life with cows, chickens, garden produce and home canning, and notes her youngest son's back-to-the-land ways.

title: Meeting Ernest; the Depression
description: She describes meeting her husband at dances and the grain scale house and courting seven years because the Depression left him out of work. Earning $100 a month, she paid her father's taxes, and remembers neighbours losing farms or taking their lives.

title: Break talk; family approval; dancing
description: After some off-topic chatter about coffee and tiredness, Bobby says her parents loved Ernest, who, having lost his own mother, adored her mother. She mourns old-time marriages of convenience and recalls dancing ballroom styles like the waltz, fox trot and turkey trot twice a week.

title: Community dances; dance cards and courtship
description: Edith Hilda Cooney recalls going to dances in nearby halls around Moscow, Idaho, and meeting young people from Garfield, Flushing, and Moscow. She explains that engaged and married people still danced with many partners and that a filled dance card depended more on dancing skill than appearance. The talk also touches on favorite songs, close partner dancing, and how central dancing was to social life.

title: Old farmhouse and first years of marriage
description: The interview turns from recreation to the farmhouse Edith and her husband chose when they were determined to farm. She describes the poor condition of the place, its old structure, stoves, repairs, and early lack of modern conveniences. The conversation also moves into their long courtship, marriage, and choice to have two children.

title: Health care; children and grandchildren; hobbies
description: Edith discusses doctors, medical costs, births, dental care, and childhood glasses during and after the Depression. She then reflects on her hopes for her children and grandchildren, emphasizing happy home lives. She also talks about collecting antiques, quilts, braided rugs, reading, and how she heard about a community presentation.

title: Politics; Pearl Harbor; family work and dairy years
description: Edith remembers her parents' opposite party loyalties and shares her views on Franklin D. Roosevelt and the Depression. She vividly recalls washing clothes in Moscow when she heard the news of Pearl Harbor, then compares that with the Kennedy assassination while she was teaching. The discussion shifts to what she contributed to her family, including financial help, teaching income, dairy work before dawn, 4-H, and prize money from the fair.

title: Home repair; antiques; returning to college
description: Edith explains how she and her husband divided renovation work, including his carpentry and her wallpapering and furniture refinishing. She says they are collectors rather than sellers and reflects on the hard but interesting dairy years. She then describes returning to university after decades away, taking courses by correspondence, and favoring math and science in teaching.

title: Marriage beliefs; well witching; rural life
description: Edith says she and her husband shaped each other's thinking without serious quarrels, though they disagreed somewhat over water witching. She recalls the struggle to find water on the farm and the successful well located through a dowsing method. The section closes with her preference for rural privacy, safety, self-entertainment, and her lack of interest in city life.

title: Origins; the West; regional differences
description: The interviewer and Edith compare where they grew up, including Michigan and upstate New York. Edith says she is from Idaho and talks about how much she loves the West and its mountains. She also notes the differences between northern and southern Idaho.
